name: Madecassic acid

card.summary: A triterpene acid from Centella asiatica (cica) that skincare brands use, usually via the whole plant extract, for soothing and skin repair.
card.note: Usually found as part of Centella extract; contact dermatitis is reported.

quick.overview:
Madecassic acid is one of four main pentacyclic triterpenes in Centella asiatica (gotu kola, "cica"), alongside asiatic acid, asiaticoside and madecassoside. It is the aglycone of madecassoside.

Cica products are used to calm and repair skin. Research is mostly on whole extracts and glycosides in wound healing and skin disease, with limited work isolating madecassic acid itself [1][3].
quick.how: It appears in creams, serums and sheet masks as part of Centella extract, typically used on redness-prone, irritated or post-procedure skin. It is not generally sold as a standalone product.
quick.risks: Topical Centella can cause contact dermatitis and irritation, and oral products have been linked to rare liver reports [11]. Cell and zebrafish studies show cytotoxic and cardiotoxic effects at lab concentrations [8][9].

lead: Madecassic acid is a pentacyclic triterpenoid, one of the main active compounds of Centella asiatica, along with asiatic acid, asiaticoside and madecassoside [1][2]. The plant has been used for centuries as an ethnomedicine, and extracts appear in cosmetic and clinical skin products [2][4].

Reviews describe Centella triterpenes as enhancing collagen synthesis, modulating inflammation and offering antioxidant protection, which underlies their use for wound healing and skin soothing [3]. For appearance, that translates to calmer, less irritated skin and support for repair after minor wounds or scars [1][3].

chain: Centella triterpenes support collagen and modulate inflammation
Irritated skin calms and wounds heal
angle.text: Madecassic acid acts alongside related Centella triterpenes in cica products used to soothe skin and support healing. It is chosen for sensitive, red or post-procedure skin.

paras: Centella products are used for wound healing, hypertrophic scars and burns in the literature [1], and in cosmetic skincare for sensitive skin [4].

Reviews describe collagen synthesis, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions of the Centella triterpenes [3][2]. Pharmacokinetic work has studied standardised oral Centella extract in healthy volunteers [5][7].

Topical use can cause contact dermatitis and irritation, and case reports describe liver disease in people taking Centella over several weeks [11]. In laboratory work, madecassic acid derivatives show cytotoxicity to cancer cells [8][10], and madecassic and asiatic acid caused cardiotoxicity in zebrafish [9].

Human trials use Centella extracts rather than madecassic acid alone. A randomised multicentre trial tested a spray film containing Centella extract (including asiatic acid, madecassic acid, asiaticoside and madecassoside) on acute wounds [6], and phase I studies assessed oral extract safety and pharmacokinetics [5][7]. Reviews summarise wound-healing trials [3][4].
